Dear Diary,
Three weeks since Farida ended it. Today I finally stopped checking her profile.
I've been a mess. I replayed every conversation, looking for the moment I ruined it. But when I read our old chats today, I saw something else: we fought about the same things again and again. She wanted to move abroad; I want to stay near my parents. She thought my volunteering was a waste of time. I thought her plans ignored mine.
We liked each other. But we didn't want the same life.
It still hurts. I cried in the bathroom at work. But I went for a run after, and called my cousin, and cooked a proper dinner for the first time in weeks.
Next time, I want to talk about values early, not just about films.
— Santosh

qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.a: Santosh felt sad but also clearer, realising they wanted different lives.

qa.a: Farida probably also felt the pull between her plans to move abroad and Santosh's wish to stay, which may be why she ended it.

grounding: In a diary a young adult recovers from a breakup and sees the value of compatible life goals.

In the small town, Jatin's family had arranged for him to meet a girl, Sneha's cousin Radhika. On paper, everything matched: same community, good jobs.
They met at a café near the bus stand. Radhika asked, "What do you do on Sundays?" Jatin said he teaches kids at the government school. She laughed. "Why waste time on that?"
Later, Jatin told his friend Varun, "She was nice. But she laughed at the one thing I care about most."
Varun said, "Does that matter more than the job match?"
Jatin thought for a long time. "Yes."
He told his parents gently that it wasn't right. His mother sighed but said, "Better you know now."

People ask how Uma and I stayed friends for ten years. I'm Kunal, by the way. Here's the honest answer: we nearly didn't.
After college, she went to Delhi, I stayed in Pune. For six months we just liked each other's posts. That's not friendship; that's being polite.

In my second year, I shared a flat with Gopika and two others. For months, I was the one doing all the dishes. I didn't say anything. I just got angrier, banging pots loudly.
One night Gopika asked, "Why are you so grumpy?" And I exploded. "Because I'm the only one who ever cleans!"

We sat down that weekend and made a rota. Gopika took dishes on weekdays; I took the bathroom. We shared groceries through a notebook.
I'm Anirban. I learnt that silent resentment makes conflict worse. Saying it early, calmly, would have saved us months.

Then my body started giving signals. Headaches every day. I stopped reading, stopped calling friends. I snapped at a junior for a tiny mistake and felt nothing afterwards.

Dear Chandrika,
You asked why I've been off the fantasy betting app. I want to be honest with you.
It started as fun: small bets on cricket with friends. Then I was checking it every hour. When I lost, I'd bet more to win it back. When I won, I felt amazing for a minute, then wanted more. I hid it from everyone.
Last month I borrowed from my roommate to cover a loss. That's when I got scared.
I told my brother. He helped me delete the app, block payments on my card, and find a counsellor who works with gambling problems. I've been off it for three weeks.
Some days I still want to check. I call you or go for a walk instead.
Thanks for asking. It helped to say it.
Lavanya

You want to know about my gaming? I'm Parul. Okay.
In second year, I'd play from ten at night till five in the morning. Online team games. I'd tell myself one more match, every match. If I stopped, I felt restless and irritable. I skipped classes. I lied to my parents about marks.
My friend Parveen noticed first. She said, "You look grey." I laughed it off.

I went to the student counselling centre that week. The counsellor explained the loop: stress, game, relief, guilt, more stress. We made a plan. Deleted the game from my laptop. Played football instead. Told my parents the truth.
It took months. I still play sometimes, but not at night.

I'm Ojas, and Sahil and I shared a room in the hostel. Last year I watched him get hooked on vaping.
At first it was one at parties. Then in the room, then in the washroom between classes. If he didn't have it, he was snappy. He spent his mess money on refills.
One night he couldn't sleep without it and was pacing. He said, "I think I can't stop."
The next day he went to the campus health centre. The doctor explained how nicotine creates cravings and gave him a quitting plan. He threw out his vape in front of me.
The first week was rough; he chewed gum constantly and was grumpy. I don't know exactly what he felt, but he kept going.

Asif had three hours to accept the internship offer from a big betting-games company. The pay was twice what anyone else in his class got.
His friend Uma said, "Take it. You'll learn so much."
Asif stared at the email. His uncle had lost his shop to gambling. He remembered the nights his aunt cried.
He called his mother. "Ammi, it's good money. But I don't think I can build something I think hurts people."
"What do you want to stand for?"
"I want to build things I'd show you proudly."
He declined the offer with ten minutes to spare. Uma thought he was crazy. The next week, he applied to an ed-tech startup for half the pay.

qa.a: Asif felt torn and uneasy, remembering the harm gambling caused his uncle's family.

qa.q: What helped Asif decide under time pressure?
qa.a: Remembering his family's experience and asking himself what he wanted to stand for.

qa.q: How does Uma see Asif's choice?
qa.a: Uma thinks he's crazy to turn down so much money.

At the office Diwali party in Gurugram, Varun's team was placing bets on who the boss would promote. Then someone suggested writing anonymous fake reviews of a rival team's work to make them look bad.
Everyone laughed and agreed. Leela, next to Varun, looked at him.
Varun felt his stomach drop. He liked his team. He wanted to belong.
But he'd told himself on his first day: I won't lie to get ahead.
"I'm out," he said quietly. "That's not fair to them."
Silence. Someone rolled their eyes. Leela said, "Me too."
The idea died. The next week, someone thanked Varun privately.

qa.q: What did someone suggest writing about the rival team?
qa.a: Anonymous fake reviews.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when his stomach dropped?
qa.a: Varun felt anxious and torn between belonging and his values.

qa.q: What helped Varun stand by his value?
qa.a: He had decided on a clear non-negotiable on his first day, so he could refuse calmly.

qa.q: How might Leela feel after saying "Me too"?
qa.a: Leela probably feels relieved and braver, having someone to stand with.

grounding: A young man sticks to his value of honesty despite peer pressure at work.

When I failed my second-year engineering exam, I locked myself in my room. I kept saying to myself, "You're useless. You'll never be an engineer."
My friend Ramesh knocked. "What are you telling yourself?"
I told him. He said, "Would you say that to me if I failed?"
"No. I'd say one exam isn't everything."
"Then say it to yourself."
It felt stupid. But I tried. "I failed. It hurts. I didn't study enough for thermodynamics. I can fix that."
I'm Jomon. I passed the re-exam. The voice in my head still gets harsh sometimes. But now I ask: would I say this to a friend?

qa.q: Which subject did Jomon not study enough for?
qa.a: Thermodynamics.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when locked in the room?
qa.a: Jomon felt ashamed and worthless after failing.

qa.q: What question from Ramesh helped Jomon change the self-talk?
qa.a: "Would you say that to me if I failed?", which reminded Jomon to use the same kind words inwardly as with a friend.

qa.q: How might Ramesh have felt helping Jomon?
qa.a: Ramesh probably felt caring and relieved when Jomon's inner voice started to soften.

grounding: A young adult learns to replace harsh self-talk with accountable, supportive self-talk.

Football coach's note, women's college team.
In today's semi-final, Rehana missed the deciding penalty. She dropped to her knees and wouldn't look at anyone. In the dressing room she said, "I ruined everything. I'm the worst player."
Vandana, our captain, sat with her. I heard her say, "You scored two goals this season that got us here. You missed one penalty. Both are true."
I told Rehana that professional players miss penalties too, and asked what she'd practise next time. She said, "Placement, not power."
Tomorrow we'll practise penalties together. I'll also check on her after the weekend. — Coach Pereira

Dear Diary,
My presentation today was a disaster. The slides froze, I forgot my second point, and my voice shook. Arnab had to jump in.
On the way home I kept thinking, "You're so stupid. Everyone saw."
Then I remembered what the counsellor told us in first year: talk to yourself like you'd talk to a friend.
So, if Arnab had done this, I'd say: "That was hard luck with the slides. You still knew the material. Next time, practise once with the projector and keep notes on a card."
Okay. That's fair. I'm going to message Arnab to thank him for covering.
— Reena

qa.a: Reena felt embarrassed and harshly critical, thinking "Everyone saw."
